item.description: An excerpt from ‘Batanagar: A Personal History of India’s Forgotten Company Town’, by Paramita Sen.

On a still October afternoon in 1934, a fleet of 12 cars starting their journey from Budge Budge trudged along a largely unpaved path known as Kasimuddin Road and arrived at an irrigation canal in a village that was no longer in use. Unable to drive further through the thickly wooded area, some of the passengers decided to walk the rest of the way. Eventually, they came upon the bank of the Hooghly, where two poles flying the Union Jack and the Czechoslovakian flag had been erected. At the centre were placed some bricks, stones and a container filled with unused mortar and a scoop decorated with flowers around its handle.

Beneath a tent close by stood Bretislav Martinec, the architect in charge of implementing František Gahura’s vision of Batanagar, and his team members, John Bartos, general manager, and Bata employees along with visitors including Czechoslovak Consul Dr Lusk, Prof Benoy Kumar Sarkar of Calcutta University, members of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce and an assortment of business people and friends from neighbouring regions. While one order seeks “to expand the definition of people who are ineligible for birthright citizenship”, another aims to prevent people from travelling to the country to give birth. The latter is described by the White House as “birth tourism”.

“That practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned,” Stephen Miller, Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy at the White House, said.

item.title: ‘Vadhandhi Season Two’ review: A juicy fleshing-out of the secrets hidden in skeletons
item.description: Andrew Louis’s Tamil series is out on Prime Video.
item.content:encoded:
The chance discovery of two skeletons seemingly closes the door on one mystery – but opens another. The rotting remains contain enough DNA evidence to convict the man already under arrest for the murders.

Mani, a young jallikattu player, is awaiting sentencing for the deaths of Venba (Deepikka Anand) and Nilavathi (Revathy S). With the evidence stacked against Mani (Yashwanth), and his refusal to defend himself, it appears that sub-inspector Moosa’s investigation is over even before it began.

But Moosa Razaa (M Sasikumar) is sceptical. He is many other things too.

He’s dogged, having fought a case to keep his beard in adherence to his faith. He’s honest. He’s fastidious. He doesn’t believe in closing a case file just to maintain a healthy conviction rate. Handed a jigsaw with every piece neatly fitted into place, Moosa is going to destroy the puzzle and start all over again.

The new season of the Tamil series Vadhandhi (Rumour) continues the overarching theme of separating facts from conjecture. The first season from 2022 on Prime Video followed the murder of 18-year-old Velonie, whose sexual objectification considerably muddled the police investigation.

item.title: ‘Ohh My Dog’ review: A smart kid and a fabulous canine deliver a parable about goodness and justice

item.content:encoded:
The new film by Amit Rai, the director of Road to Sangam and Oh My God 2, looks for the divine in the canine. Ohh My Dog is about the bond between humans and their four-legged friends who give more than they ever get in return.

The Hindi film, which is out in cinemas, follows two stories. In a small town in Assam, young Apu’s pet Momo goes missing. Police officer Mohammed (Vijay Mishra) starts investigating, but he’s several steps behind the sharp-brained, tech-savvy Apu (Maahi Rai).

Not for nothing is Apu named after the hero of Pather Panchali. A large poster of Satyajit Ray in Apu’s home suggests that Apu is a younger version of Ray’s fictional detective Feluda. Apu and his tuition teacher Krishna (Sulakhyana Baruah) accompany Mohammed on the quest for Momo, with Apu leading the way.

item.title: The dark side of the booming Indian market for weight-loss drugs
item.description: Scroll found unauthorised doctors prescribing the medicines in salons and online sellers and chemists agreeing to sell it even without a prescription.
item.content:encoded:
Saloni Khera, a social media manager in Mumbai, gained 30 kg in just six months after the Covid-19 pandemic.

A combination of factors were at work. She had long Covid, a condition in which the virus leaves behind a trail of health problems. She was pre-diabetic and also had a hormonal disorder.

She weighed 153.5 kg.

Her attempts at losing weight through multiple diet regimens – even drinking only water for a week – had failed. “If I lost 15 kg, I gained 25 kg back,” she said.

People with chronic obesity, a lifelong disorder like diabetes or hypertension, can gain weight rapidly, putting pressure on their heart. This can have a cascading effect on their health.

Last year, Khera consulted a gynaecologist in Ahmedabad as she and her husband began to think about having a child. “I wanted to be fit to be able to do it,” the 35-year-old told Scroll.

The gynaecologist referred her to an endocrinologist who advised her to reduce weight first. He suggested she try the weight-loss drug – Mounjaro – an injectable that can help reduce over 20% body weight.

item.title: An evolutionary model that predates Darwin’s natural selection is making a comeback
item.description: Lamarckism contended that an organism may acquire characteristics in response to its environment and pass these on.
item.content:encoded:
Evolution is a fact of life. So much so that even the theory of evolution is evolving. Lately, a centuries-old discredited idea has been making a strong comeback. It helps us explain scientific observations that according to standard evolutionary theory should be impossible.

I’m referring to Lamarckism, named after theoretical proposals from French biologist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1809. Lamarckism stands for the hypothesis that parents of a given organism may acquire or improve certain characteristics during their lifetimes in response to the demands of their environment. And they then somehow transmit those characteristics to their offspring, making those better able to cope with the same demands too.

Lamarck sought to explain why organisms and their environments fit so well together, and how organisms change over time, as observed in the fossil record. Of course, an alternative explanation was provided by Charles Darwin (and others) half a century later. Darwin’s ideas were built around natural selection, which says that some individuals within a species are born with differences that lead them to perform better and therefore reproduce more than others.

The RSS is the parent organisation of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Addressing an event at the Nita Mukesh Ambani Centre in Mumbai, Bhagwat said that the grievances of the youngsters were genuine and reflected shortcomings in the education system.

“If the Gen Z is agitating, they certainly are not anti-nationals,” NDTV quoted Bhagwat as saying. “They are our own people, our next generation.”

He said that while previous generations did as told, the “Gen Z and Gen Alpha want logical answers”.

“Gen Z” refers to persons born between the late 1990s and 2010. “Gen Alpha” are persons born between 2010 and 2024.

item.title: Cockroach movement claims victory but the odds are stacked against India’s youngsters
item.description: Four main issues of fairness in education and employment need to be addressed.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past few weeks, young people have mobilised to protest India’s broken education system, against the background of a shortage of job opportunities.

The protests were initially sparked by the cancellation of a medical school entrance exam after questions were leaked, leading some despondent young people to take their own lives. The movement repurposed the image of a cockroach as their symbol – inspired by a comment by India’s chief justice, allegedly comparing jobless young people to “cockroaches”. Humour and satire were integral to the recent unrest.

On Saturday, the cockroach movement claimed its biggest victory since the protests began with the resignation of India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

But this move will only do so much. These issues did not appear overnight, nor can they be easily fixed.

Decades of frustration

Irregularities and shortcomings in education, as well as rampant unemployment, have been major issues in northern India since at least the early 1970s. One of the main reasons for this is the economic growth that occurred in the late 20th century was not accompanied by broad-based investment in education. It also failed to create jobs in the private sector, leaving many young people dependent on government jobs.

item.title: Rs 557 crore spent on PM Modi’s foreign trips since 2021
item.description: In 2026, the government incurred an expenditure of Rs 74.5 crore for six official tours that covered 13 countries.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government has spent Rs 557.5 crore on foreign trips made by Prime Minister Narendra Modi since 2021.

While Rs 36.1 crore was spent on the prime minister’s foreign visits in 2021, the expenditure was Rs 55.8 crore in 2022. Modi undertook fewer trips in the two years amid the Covid-19 pandemic.

In 2023, Rs 93.6 crore was spent on his visits abroad, followed by Rs 109.5 crore in 2024 and Rs 187.8 crore in 2025.

The government has spent Rs 74.5 crore in 2026 so far on six trips that covered 13 countries.

The most expensive trip by Modi during this period was to the United States in February 2025, which cost more than Rs 25.5 crore, the Ministry of External Affairs informed Parliament on Thursday.

In 2026, the largest amount of funds was spent on the prime minister’s trip to Norway in May, which cost Rs 17 crore.

The data released by the ministry did not specify what the money was spent on.

However, in a submission made to the Rajya Sabha in March 2025 about Modi’s foreign visits, the government had said that the cost includes the expenditure on accommodations for the prime minister’s delegation, transportation, security and hardware, venue charges and “miscellaneous” expenses.

item.title: Can the Indian Knowledge Systems be defended from pseudoscience?
item.description: Indian science can only be strengthened when its boundaries are clearly separated from culture, belief and pseudoscience.
item.content:encoded:
Last summer, I taught a course called Quantitative Reasoning and Mathematical Thinking. Much of it was focussed on the history of mathematics in India: numbers in the Vedas, the geometry of the Sulbasutras and the work of Pingala, Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Bhaskaracharya, and Ramanujan.

Teaching this course was among the pleasures of my year.

It was also difficult. A large part of what I did in that classroom was not teaching what Indian mathematicians had achieved, but separating it from what they did not.

We read SG Dani’s Myths and Reality: On ‘Vedic Mathematics’ to see why a set of arithmetic shortcuts compiled and published in 1965 has nothing to do with the Vedas, and Rick Briggs’s Knowledge Representation in Sanskrit and Artificial Intelligence to trace where the claim that Sanskrit is “the language of AI” or the most logical programming language ever, came from – and to see that the paper itself says no such thing.

item.title: How the BJP stole the month of Sawan
item.description: In India’s Hindutva calendar, there is now only the ‘holy’, ‘sacred’ or ‘auspicious’ month of Shravan.
item.content:encoded:
There was a time when we called the monsoon month of Sawan by its name. In traditional lore, with its arrival, swings would appear in orchards. The air would be filled with the melodies of the kajri folk form and Raag Malhar. The Earth changed its attire as nature draped herself in a green veil.

Sawan meant relief and hope.

For farmers, Sawan is still Sawan. Even today, they call it by that name. Few other lives are bound to rain and drought as intimately as theirs. They await Sawan with particular longing. They know that the rhythm of cultivation changes with it.

Farmers know what the month means for paddy, maize, jowar, chana, black gram, cotton and other crops. Many of their festivals, too, fall in this month. There is Teej. There is Nag Panchami. The agricultural calendar and the Hindu ritual calendar have long lived together.

But we no longer inhabit that older sense of time. We now live within an official Hindutva calendar. It is no longer Sawan that begins but the auspicious month of Shravan. Every mention of Shravan must now be preceded by adjectives such as “holy, sacred or auspicious”.

item.title: Misinformation about health and wellness can be convincing – here is how to spot it
item.description: Claims spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.
item.content:encoded:
Recent reports have highlighted AI-generated “doctors” spreading dubious health advice to millions of social media users. Fabricated wellness trends can travel just as quickly. A supposed “pink jelly” weight-loss treatment, for example, reportedly fooled at least one celebrity.

These examples gain credibility in different ways. Influencers can appear familiar and sincere, while AI-generated doctors can look like qualified professionals. Neither familiarity nor the appearance of expertise tells us whether a medical claim is accurate.

Turning to friends and family for health advice is understandable. They may know our circumstances in ways that a healthcare professional cannot during a brief appointment. They can provide emotional support and practical help, and their advice is usually well meant. But somebody can care about us, speak honestly and still be wrong.

Truth and trust

My own research and wider research on digital health misinformation shows that trust can play an important part in deciding which claims people accept. Trust in clinicians and scientific institutions is generally associated with lower susceptibility to false health claims. Misinformation can nevertheless spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.

The Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy Committee on Wednesday kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks. The Monetary Policy Committee reviews the rate every two months.

The committee had cut the repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.50% in December and kept it unchanged in February, April and June.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Basis points are used to describe the percentage change in the value of a financial instrument.

Central banks usually reduce repo rates to stimulate economic growth by making borrowing cheaper for individuals and businesses. This translates to lower equated monthly instalments for borrowers.

On Wednesday, the policy committee said that it had decided to maintain its monetary policy stance as “neutral”.

A neutral stance means that the Reserve Bank remained flexible in adjusting policy rates based on prevailing economic conditions.

item.title: When you hit ‘delete’, what really happens to your data?
item.description: There is a pressing need for provision of concise, accessible and clear information about how deletion really works.
item.content:encoded:
Deletion is a common part of modern life. We send files and folders to the recycle bin all the time, and often get rid of unwanted personal accounts. But do you know what really happens when you hit the “delete” button?

The process of deletion is often poorly explained by tech providers. Lack of transparency around how requests are processed, and the absence of clear confirmation that data has been removed, are frequently highlighted in research.

These issues are not limited to operating systems. On social media platforms and a wide range of subscription services, deletion mechanisms are often just as unclear. Such misconceptions can have serious implications for the wellbeing of users, exposing them to security and privacy vulnerabilities.

A further complication is that many users fear losing data, files, photos and videos through accidental deletion – a condition dubbed “diagraphephobia”. Though this is not a recognised pathology, studies of digital hoarding behaviour show that some people get very anxious at the thought of losing or accidentally deleting personal information such as photos and music.

Such concerns extend the amount of personal data that sits untended but undeleted, ready for potential misappropriation.

Being confined to the sal-dominated (Shorea robusta) tropical moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forests in India, and the sub-tropical and temperate broad-leaved forests in the India – Bhutan landscape, the golden langur stands out as the most restricted colobine (leaf-eating primate) species in India. Although described by earlier naturalists such as RB Pemberton and CM Inglis and co-workers during the 19th century as “cream colored monkey” and “Sankosh cream langurs”, the credit for suggesting that it could be a new species goes to EP Gee, a British tea planter and conservationist living in Assam. It was formally described in 1956 by H Khajuria of the Zoological Survey of India and named Presbytis geei in honour of Gee.

The golden langur is a medium-sized primate. Males weigh 10-12 kg and females 9.5-10 kg. They are less sexually dimorphic than other colobines such as grey langurs (Semnopithecus spp). Based on phylogeny and biogeography, T Wangchuk, a Bhutanese biologist, opined that Trachypithecus geei and T pileatus (capped langurs) branched off from an ancestral Trachypithecus from South Asia. In addition, the Sankosh River and Pele La mountain system in central Bhutan isolated a population of capped langurs during a warming period in central Bhutan, and this population later specialised into the morphologically distinct golden langur.

item.title: Bali’s fishing canoes are vanishing as tourism changes Indonesia’s coastline
item.description: The traditional boats with colourful carvings of the mythical elephant-fish on their prows represent centuries of maritime heritage.
item.content:encoded:
Five decades ago, Bali’s coastline was adorned with traditional fishing canoes with colourful carvings of mythical elephant-fish. Where did they go?

The disappearance of these canoes tells a much bigger story about how tourism, collecting and coastal change are reshaping Indonesia’s living maritime heritage – and why preserving these traditions matters.

The boats that once lined Bali’s beaches

Before Bali became one of the worlds’ most popular tourist destinations, fishing villages lined the beaches of Benoa, Nusa Dua and Sanur, along the island’s southern coast.

Generations of fishers built and sailed jukung pelasan – traditional timber double-outrigger sailing canoes with colourful carved gajah mina (elephant-fish) prows.

The gajah mina is a creature in Balinese Hindu tradition with the head of an elephant and the body of a fish. Symbolising unity and harmony between land and sea, it is said to protect crews during voyages and provide safe passage.

These were not just fishing boats; they were central to daily life in southern Bali.

The jukung were symbols of status and community identity. They embodied generations of craftsmanship, spiritual belief and maritime knowledge. They expressed the economic, social and spiritual life of Bali’s coastal communities, and reflected the enduring relationship between its people and the sea.

Today, however, only a handful remain.

He also claimed that Rs 1,400 crore had been “stolen” from the Ram temple in Ayodhya.

The remarks came amid a row over the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Ram temple in Uttar Pradesh.

On Sunday, citing a letter purportedly written by eight temple trustees to Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde, Thackeray claimed that employees at Siddhivinayak temple had siphoned off donations from collection boxes.

He also claimed that the temple’s weekly donations were below Rs 50 lakh before the alleged theft came to light, but increased to about Rs 1.5 crore after those allegedly involved were caught.

Sada Sarvankar, chairperson of the Siddhivinayak Temple Trust and a leader of the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, said that nine temple employees had been arrested in connection with the alleged theft, PTI reported.

item.title: Kerala: 15 killed in rain-related incidents, seven missing
item.description: The state government will provide Rs 10,000 in funeral expenses to the families of those who died, said Chief Minister VD Satheesan.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in rain-related incidents in Kerala has risen to 15, PTI quoted Chief Minister VD Satheesan as saying on Monday.

While he did not specify the period in which the deaths took place, the state has been receiving heavy and incessant rainfall since Friday, triggering flash floods and landslides.

Satheesan said on Monday that seven persons were missing amid the rains. Of these, two persons each were missing from Kollam and Kannur, and one each in Malappuram, Idukki and Muvattupuzha.

Malappuram had reported four deaths, while three persons died in Kottayam district. Two deaths each were reported in Ernakulam and Kollam, and one person each died in Idukki, Muvattupuzha and Kannur.

The chief minister announced that the state government will provide Rs 10,000 in funeral expenses to the families of those who died. Persons returning home from relief camps would receive Rs 10,000 as an immediate measure.

Additionally, an ex gratia of Rs 8 lakh was announced for the families of those who died. A compensation of Rs 12 lakh will be given to those who lost their homes and land due to landslides. Rs 6 lakh will be provided for families to rebuild their homes, said Satheesan.

item.title: Youth protests: Supreme Court clarifies states can withdraw FIRs against demonstrators
item.description: The statement came after the Centre submitted that it was ‘serious’ about its assurance that no coercive action will be taken against student protesters.

The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that states can withdraw first information reports filed against youth protesters wherever permissible, in accordance with the law, Live Law reported.

The clarification came in response to concerns raised by petitioners that the court’s July 28 order, which allowed states to continue investigations into the FIRs, could hinder the withdrawal of cases. They argued that closing the FIRs was part of the Union government’s promise to leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign to end the protests.

It also came after the Union government submitted that it was “serious” about its assurance that amnesty would be granted to students who had participated in demonstrations, The Hindu reported.

In its July 28 order, the Supreme Court had directed that minors who had been detained should be released and no coercive action should be taken against protesting students as long as they did not have any “criminal antecedents”.

On Monday, the bench also clarified that the term “criminal antecedents” in the order referred only to “grave and heinous offences”.

item.title: Bangladesh: Hindu monk Chinmoy Krishna Das gets bail, will remain in jail in four other cases

Bangladesh’s High Court on Sunday granted bail to Hindu religious leader Chinmoy Krishna Das in two cases, The Daily Star reported. However, he will not be released from prison as he is accused in four other cases.

The monk, who was formerly associated with the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, has been in jail since November 25, 2024. He was arrested for allegedly disrespecting Bangladesh’s national flag during a rally on October 25 that year in Chittagong.

He is the spokesperson of the Sammilito Sanatani Jagaron Jote, an organisation that advocates for the rights of Hindus and other minorities in Bangladesh.

The two cases in which he was granted bail on Sunday pertain to attempted murder and obstructing police officers from discharging their duties.

The murder case is about the death of a public prosecutor during clashes that broke out on November 26, 2024, between Das’ supporters and lawyers near the Chattogram Court, when his bail petition was rejected.

The police alleged that the Hindu leader’s followers blocked the prison van in which he was travelling, prompting the clash during which a lawyer, Saiful Islam Alif, was hacked to death.

Following the transfer, the paper leak cases, including those related to the 2026 undergraduate National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test, will be heard by Special Judge Ajay Gupta.

Gupta had been hearing the NEET case before the fast-track court was constituted, The Indian Express reported.

If one looks beyond the merits of the student unrest at Jantar Mantar, beyond the politics, the partisanship and the competing narratives and reflect solely on the conduct of the policing forces at the venue, one is left with a profound sense of unease.

This reflection comes from someone who has worn the uniform, led troops in some of the most challenging circumstances during the height of insurgency in the Kashmir Valley and witnessed first-hand the pressures, provocations and split-second decisions that confront those entrusted with maintaining order in volatile situations.

There is a deep understanding of the difficult circumstances in which uniformed personnel often operate, the dangers they face and the emotional and operational pressures that can arise when confronted by crowds, unrest, or hostility.

On Sunday, student leader Devendra Nath Mahto began an indefinite hunger strike at the stadium.

The protesters have demanded the cancellation of the 14th Jharkhand Public Service Commission Combined Preliminary Test held on April 19, PTI reported.

They have also sought independent inquiries by the Central Bureau of Investigation and the Enforcement Directorate into alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission, the news agency reported.
